paras: The Greenville shooting of Huston Herbert was an exchange of gunfire on the night of August 11, 1915, in Greenville, Alabama, between Huston Herbert, a Black man, and a party of county and city officers who had come to his home in search of his brother. About twenty-three revolver shots were fired, but no one was reported hit, and neither Herbert brother had been taken by the following evening.

The officers were looking for Joe Herbert, whom the Montgomery Advertiser described as an escaped convict and as Huston Herbert's brother. The party consisted of Sheriff Harrison of Butler County, three of his deputies, Greenville Chief of Police J. R. Porterfield and Policeman Daniel, who went to the Herbert home "heavily armed" because, the paper said, the brothers had "a reputation of being desperate."

According to the Advertiser's Greenville correspondent, Huston Herbert "did not like the presence of the officers in the house" and left by the rear door, where several officers were stationed. The paper said that he opened fire on them and that the officers shot at him as he fled. Apparently none of the bullets took effect, and none of the officers was hit.

Late on August 12 neither Huston nor Joe Herbert had been captured, though the officers were pursuing them and information received in Greenville held that both would be in the sheriff's hands before midnight. No report of a capture, charge or trial of either man appears in the coverage.

The shooting is known from a single short special to the Montgomery Advertiser, printed on page 3 on August 13 under the headline "MANY EMPTY PISTOLS, BUT NO ONE IS HURT." The item gave the officers' account as fact, including the statement that Herbert fired first, and called both brothers "negroes" with a reputation for being "desperate." No other white paper and no Black paper was found to have reported the episode.

reader.title: Greenville shooting of Huston Herbert
bases: County and city officers searching a Black family's home for an escaped convict fired on Huston Herbert as he fled, after what the paper says was his own fire on them (A1).
Only one report, a special to the Montgomery Advertiser, describes the shooting; no second white or any Black-press account was found (A1).

accounts.gist: Officers went to the Herbert home seeking escaped convict Joe Herbert; Huston, displeased at their presence, left by the rear door and fired on officers stationed there, who shot at him as he fled; no one was hit.

framing.detail: The Advertiser treated the shooting lightly ('MANY EMPTY PISTOLS, BUT NO ONE IS HURT'), said 'the negroes have a reputation of being desperate' to explain the officers' heavy arms, and reported Huston firing first as fact.
